tagline: The visions, sign-acts, and oracles of a priest exiled to Babylon, who saw God's glory leave Jerusalem's temple and saw it return.
overview:
Ezekiel was a priest who never served in the temple. He was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and five years later, living among the exiles beside the Kebar canal, he saw the heavens open and the glory of the LORD come to him in a foreign land. For the next twenty years or more he spoke to a displaced community that clung to the hope that Jerusalem could not fall and that their stay in Babylon would be short. His first task was to destroy that hope. His second, after the city fell in 587 or 586 BC, was to give them a better one.

The book is full of strange and memorable things: a vision of living creatures, wheels, and a throne above a crystal expanse; a scroll eaten like honey; a prophet who lies on his side for months beside a clay model of a besieged city; the glory of God rising from the temple and departing east; a valley of dry bones that stands up as an army; and a final vision of a new temple from which a river flows out to heal the Dead Sea. Behind all of it is one conviction repeated more than sixty times: that people and nations will know that I am the LORD.

Ezekiel matters because it shows God's holiness and his faithfulness at the same moment. God judges his people because he is holy and will not share his house with idols. He restores them for the same reason, for the sake of his holy name, and he promises what they cannot produce themselves: a new heart, a new spirit, and his own presence dwelling among them again.
author:
The book presents itself as the work of Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest (1:3), and most of it is written in the first person with precise dates. Jewish and Christian tradition has accepted it as his. A line in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says the men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, which most take to mean that a later body put the collection into its final written form, not that they composed it.

In the early twentieth century some critical scholars assigned large parts of the book to later writers. Most scholars today credit the core of the book to the prophet himself, though they differ on how much later shaping it received. Walther Zimmerli, in his major commentary, argued that disciples of Ezekiel extended and applied his words in a kind of school. Moshe Greenberg, in his commentary, argued that the book reads best as a coherent composition largely from the prophet's own hand. Both views take the dates, the setting, and the prophet's voice seriously.
date: Ezekiel is the most carefully dated of the prophetic books. More than a dozen oracles carry a date counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The first vision comes in the fifth year of that exile, in the summer of 593 BC (1:2). News of Jerusalem's fall reaches the exiles in the twelfth year (33:21). The temple vision is dated to the twenty-fifth year, about 573 BC (40:1), and the latest dated oracle, a short word about Egypt, to the twenty-seventh year, about 571 BC (29:17). The book was probably gathered into its present form during the exile, soon after its last oracle, though scholars who see more editorial expansion allow for a longer process. The thirtieth year in 1:1 is unexplained; many take it as the prophet's age when he was called.
setting:
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II was the great power of the day. In 597 BC it took King Jehoiachin, the royal family, officials, soldiers, and craftsmen into exile (2 Kings 24:10-16), and Ezekiel went with them. The exiles were settled in communities in southern Mesopotamia, including Tel-abib by the Kebar canal (3:15). Babylonian business records from the city of Nippur mention a canal by the name Kabar, which is probably the same waterway. The exiles had their own houses and elders (8:1) and some freedom to gather, but they were far from the land and the temple.

Back in Jerusalem, King Zedekiah ruled as a Babylonian vassal and was soon plotting rebellion with Egypt's help. Prophets in both places promised a quick deliverance. Ezekiel, like Jeremiah in Jerusalem, insisted that the city would fall, and in 587 or 586 BC it did. His later oracles address a community that has lost everything it had trusted: city, king, land, and temple. They also address the nations around Judah, especially Tyre and Egypt, whose pride and opportunism the prophet judges.
purpose: Ezekiel's book had two jobs, one before the fall of Jerusalem and one after. Before the fall, it aimed to strip the exiles of false confidence: the temple would not save a city that had filled it with idols, and God was not bound to a building. The famous vision of the glory leaving the temple (chapters 8 to 11) makes that point. After the fall, the book aimed to keep the survivors from despair by showing that the same God who judged would restore, not because Israel deserved it but for the sake of his name. It also calls every hearer to personal responsibility (chapter 18) and to the hope of a new heart and spirit given by God (chapter 36).
story: Ezekiel belongs to the exile, the long gap between the fall of Jerusalem (told in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah) and the return under Persian rule (told in Ezra and Nehemiah). He is a younger contemporary of Jeremiah and a contemporary of Daniel. He names a righteous and wise Daniel (14:14; 28:3), though scholars differ on whether that figure is the Daniel of the book of Daniel or the ancient Danel of Canaanite legend. Where Jeremiah watched the end from inside Jerusalem and Lamentations mourned it, Ezekiel interpreted it from Babylon. His visions of a restored people, a united kingdom under a Davidic shepherd, and a renewed temple shaped the hopes of the returning exiles and, in turn, the imagery of the New Testament.
christ: Several of Ezekiel's great promises come to rest in Jesus. In chapter 34 God condemns the shepherds who fed themselves, promises to shepherd his flock himself, and in the same breath promises one shepherd, his servant David; Jesus calls himself the good shepherd in John 10 against that background. The promise of a new heart and a new spirit within (36:26-27) belongs with Jeremiah's new covenant, and the New Testament sees it fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit. The glory that left the temple returns, and John says of Jesus that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us and that we saw his glory (John 1:14). The river from the temple becomes Jesus' picture of the Spirit flowing from within believers (John 7:37-39) and Revelation's river of the water of life (Revelation 22:1-2). Ezekiel's title, son of man, mostly means simply a mortal, and the New Testament's use of that title for Jesus draws more directly on Daniel 7; but the humble prophet who bears his people's iniquity in chapter 4 is a real, if partial, pattern of the one who would bear it fully.
reading:
Ezekiel mixes several kinds of writing: visions (chapters 1 to 3, 8 to 11, 37, and 40 to 48), sign-acts in which the prophet acts out his message, long allegories (chapters 16, 17, 23), legal-style case teaching (chapter 18), oracles against nations, and detailed architectural description. Take each on its own terms. The visions use deliberately cautious language (the likeness of, the appearance of) and are not meant to be drawn as diagrams. The allegories of chapters 16 and 23 use harsh sexual imagery for idolatry; they shock on purpose, and readers should notice that they condemn the people's unfaithfulness, not women as such.

Watch for the dates, which place each oracle in the unfolding crisis, and for the refrains: son of man, they will know that I am the LORD, and the glory of the LORD. Follow the glory through the book: it appears by the Kebar (chapter 1), departs from the temple toward the east (chapters 10 and 11), and returns from the east to fill a new temple (43:1-5). That movement is the book's spine. Jewish tradition treated chapter 1 and the closing temple vision with special caution, and readers today should resist two opposite errors: dismissing the visions as unintelligible, and filling them with speculative detail the text doesn't give.

structure.title: The call by the Kebar canal
structure.summary: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD on a mobile throne, is commissioned as a prophet to a rebellious house, eats a scroll, and is appointed a watchman.

structure.title: Judgment on Jerusalem
structure.summary: Sign-acts and oracles announce the siege and fall of the city. In a vision the prophet sees idolatry in the temple and watches the glory of God depart. Allegories, case law on responsibility, and laments follow, ending on the day the siege begins and the prophet's wife dies.

structure.title: Oracles against the nations
structure.summary: Judgment on Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and above all Egypt, nations that gloated over Judah or trusted in their own power.

structure.title: Restoration promised
structure.summary: After news of the city's fall, the prophet's mouth is opened. God promises a true shepherd, a new heart and spirit, the resurrection of the nation from dry bones, the reunion of Israel and Judah, and final victory over Gog.

structure.title: The new temple and the returning glory
structure.summary: A vision of a restored temple and land. The glory of the LORD returns from the east, a river flows from the sanctuary to bring life, and the city is named The LORD is there.

themes.title: The holiness and glory of God
themes.body: Ezekiel is a priest, and he sees everything in terms of holiness: what is clean and unclean, what honors God's presence and what defiles it. The glory of the LORD is the visible radiance of God's presence. Its departure from a defiled temple is the book's darkest moment, and its return to a purified one is its climax.

themes.title: They will know that I am the LORD
themes.body: The refrain appears throughout the book, after judgment and after restoration alike. The goal of God's action in history is that Israel and the nations will recognize who he is. God acts for the sake of his name, which means for the truth about himself to be seen.

themes.title: Judgment without false hope
themes.body: Ezekiel confronts the belief that God's people are safe because of their temple, city, or ancestry. His sign-acts make the coming siege vivid, and his oracles trace the guilt of Jerusalem back through its whole history. Judgment is not arbitrary; it answers idolatry, bloodshed, and injustice.

themes.title: Personal responsibility
themes.body: Against the proverb that the children suffer for their fathers' sins, Ezekiel insists that each person answers for his own life and that anyone who turns from wickedness will live (chapter 18). The watchman passages (3:16-21; 33:1-9) apply the same principle to the prophet's own duty to warn.

themes.title: New heart, new life, new presence
themes.body: The restoration Ezekiel promises goes deeper than a return to the land. God will cleanse his people, give them a heart of flesh in place of stone, put his Spirit within them, raise the nation from death, and dwell among them forever.

keyChapters.why: The inaugural vision of the glory of the LORD on a throne above the living creatures, shown to an exile far from the temple.
The glory rises from the temple and moves to its threshold and east gate, the beginning of God's departure from a defiled house.
The classic statement that each person answers for his own sin and that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls them to turn and live.
God judges Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David, the background to Jesus as the good shepherd.
The promise of cleansing, a new heart, and God's Spirit within his people, for the sake of his holy name.
The valley of dry bones: God's breath brings a dead nation to life, and two sticks become one kingdom.
The glory of the LORD returns from the east and fills the new temple, reversing the departure of chapters 10 and 11.

parts.body:
Ezekiel was a priest who never served in the temple. He was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and five years later, living among the exiles by the River Kebar, he saw ‘visions of God’ (1:1). For more than twenty years he spoke to a displaced people who believed Jerusalem could not fall and their exile would be short.

His first task was to take that false hope away. Through visions, strange acted signs and long poems, he told them the city would fall, and why. His second task, after the news came that it had fallen, was to give them a truer hope: a shepherd, a new heart, dry bones standing up as an army, and a temple from which a river of life flows.

Behind all of it runs one refrain, repeated more than sixty times: ‘you will know that I am the LORD’ (6:7). God judges his people because he is holy, and he restores them for the sake of his holy name.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II was the great power of the day. In 597 BC it took King Jehoiachin, the royal family, officials and craftsmen into exile, and Ezekiel went with them. The exiles were settled in southern Mesopotamia, at places such as Tel-abib by the Kebar canal (3:15). They had houses and elders, and some freedom to gather, but they were far from the land and the temple.

In Jerusalem, Zedekiah ruled as Babylon's vassal and was soon plotting rebellion with Egypt's help. Prophets in both places promised quick deliverance. Ezekiel, like Jeremiah in Jerusalem, said the city would fall. The siege began in January 588 BC on the usual reckoning (24:1), and the city was taken in 587 or 586 BC. News reached the exiles about January 585 BC (33:21). His later words speak to a people who had lost city, king, land and temple, and to the nations around them, above all Tyre and Egypt.

The book presents itself as the work of ‘Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi’ (1:3), and most of it is written in the first person with exact dates. Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as his. A line in the Babylonian Talmud says the men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, which most take to mean that a later body gave the collection its final written form.

In the early twentieth century some critical scholars gave large parts of the book to later writers. Most scholars today credit its core to the prophet himself, and they differ on how much later shaping it received. Walther Zimmerli argued that disciples extended and applied his words; Moshe Greenberg argued that the book reads best as a coherent work largely from the prophet's own hand.

Ezekiel is the most carefully dated of the prophetic books. The first vision is in the summer of 593 BC (1:2), the temple vision about 573 BC (40:1), and the last dated word, about Egypt, about 571 BC (29:17). The thirtieth year of 1:1 is unexplained; many take it as the prophet's age when he was called.

The book moves in four parts. Chapters 1 to 3 are the call by the Kebar canal. Chapters 4 to 24 announce judgment on Jerusalem, through acted signs, visions, allegories, case teaching and laments, ending on the day the siege began. Chapters 25 to 32 are words against the nations, especially Tyre and Egypt. Chapters 33 to 48 turn to restoration after the news of the city's fall: a shepherd, a new heart, the dry bones, the defeat of Gog, and a long vision of a new temple and land.

Take each kind of writing on its own terms. The visions speak cautiously, of the likeness and the appearance of things, and are not diagrams. The allegories of chapters 16 and 23 use harsh sexual imagery for a city's idolatry, on purpose. Chapter 18 argues like a case in law. Watch the dates, and watch the glory of the LORD: it appears by the Kebar (chapter 1), leaves the temple toward the east (chapters 10 and 11), and returns from the east to fill a new temple (43:1-5). That movement is the book's spine.

In the fifth year of the exile, Ezekiel saw a storm from the north, four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne, and on the throne a figure like a man surrounded by brightness. ‘This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD’ (1:28). Notice how carefully he speaks. He describes the likeness of the appearance, never God himself.

The point was startling for exiles who thought God lived only in Jerusalem. The throne has wheels. God's glory comes to them in a foreign land, by a canal in Babylon. Then God sends Ezekiel to ‘a rebellious nation’ (2:3), whether they listen or not, gives him a scroll to eat, and makes him ‘a watchman for the house of Israel’ (3:17), responsible to warn them.

parts.h: Signs, and a city that would fall
parts.body:
Ezekiel did more than speak. He drew Jerusalem on a brick and laid siege to it, lay on his side for many days, cooked rationed bread, shaved his head and divided the hair, and packed his bags for exile. These acted signs made the coming siege visible to people who would not believe it.

In chapter 8 he is carried in a vision to Jerusalem and shown idolatry inside the temple itself: an image at the gate, elders burning incense to pictures of creatures, women weeping for Tammuz, men bowing to the sun. In chapters 10 and 11 the glory of the LORD rises from the temple and leaves the city to the east. God had not been driven out. He had withdrawn from a house his people had filled with idols.

Even here there is promise. To the exiles, whom Jerusalem's people despised, God says, ‘I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh’ (11:19).

Chapters 16 and 23 are among the most painful in the Bible. Chapter 16 pictures Jerusalem as an abandoned baby whom God rescued, raised and married, who then gave herself to other lovers, meaning other gods and foreign powers. Chapter 23 pictures Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, unfaithful in the same way. Both use harsh sexual images, and both end with the wife exposed and punished by her lovers.

These are pictures of a city and a covenant. The wife is a people, her lovers are idols and the nations she trusted, and the punishment is what invasion would do to the city. Interpreters weigh them differently. Some, many feminist interpreters among them, argue that the imagery, whatever its purpose, has shaped harmful attitudes and must be read critically. Others stress that it describes God's judgment on a nation and never permits anyone to treat a woman this way. Both agree that using these chapters to justify mistreating women is a grave misuse.

So it must be said plainly. These chapters give no warrant for anyone to shame, strip, threaten or harm any woman, and no one may use them to say a woman deserves to be hurt. And chapter 16 does not end in judgment. It ends with God remembering his covenant and making an everlasting one (16:60).

The exiles had a proverb: the fathers eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. They meant that they were paying for their parents' sins, and that nothing they did could change it. In chapter 18 God forbids the proverb. ‘The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father’ (18:20).

The chapter walks through three generations, a righteous man, his violent son and a grandson who turns back, and each is judged by his own life. A wicked person who turns will live; his past will not be remembered against him. ‘Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?’ (18:23).

The chapter is a call to turn, not a rule for explaining anyone's suffering. It does not say that every hardship is a deserved punishment, and it gives no one the right to read another person's pain that way. Its last word is “So repent and live!” (18:32).

Chapters 25 to 32 turn to Judah's neighbors. Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia are judged for gloating and taking revenge when Jerusalem fell. Tyre, the rich island port, is pictured as a splendid ship that sinks, and its king as one who claimed to be a god. Egypt's Pharaoh is a great monster of the Nile and a cedar that is cut down.

The common charge is pride: trusting in wealth, power and cleverness instead of the LORD. The judgment is God's, and these chapters are not a model for any people's revenge on another, then or now. Some details raise honest questions; Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for years without destroying it, and Ezekiel himself records a later word that his army got no wages from Tyre (29:18). The notes on those chapters set out how interpreters read that.

parts.h: A shepherd, a new heart, and dry bones
parts.body:
When the news came, “The city has been taken!” (33:21), Ezekiel's message turned. God condemns the shepherds who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises, ‘I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out’ (34:11). He will set over them ‘one shepherd, My servant David’ (34:23).

He will act, he says, not for their sake ‘but for My holy name’ (36:22). ‘I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh’ (36:26).

Then the valley of dry bones. ‘Son of man, can these bones come to life?’ (37:3). At God's word they come together, flesh covers them, and breath enters them. God explains: ‘these bones are the whole house of Israel’ (37:11), a people who said their hope was gone. Many Christians have also read the vision in the light of the resurrection of the dead; that is a reading, since the New Testament does not quote the chapter.

Chapters 38 and 39 describe Gog, of the land of Magog, leading many nations against a restored and peaceful Israel, and God himself defeating them on the mountains of Israel. The weapons burn for seven years, and the dead are buried for seven months, so that the land is cleansed.

Christians and Jews read these chapters in different ways, and this site takes no side. Some read Gog historically, as a figure drawn from a real ruler or people of Ezekiel's world. Some read the chapters as a prediction of a battle still to come near the end of history. Others read them as a symbolic picture of every power that rises against God's people, and of God's final victory. Revelation takes up the names Gog and Magog for the nations gathered at the end (Revelation 20:8).

On every reading, these chapters identify no modern nation, person or event, and they set no date.

parts.h: The temple vision and the river
parts.body:
In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, about 573 BC, Ezekiel was taken in a vision to a very high mountain and shown a temple, measured gate by gate by a man with a measuring rod (chapters 40 to 42). Then ‘the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east’ (43:4), returning the way it had left. Laws for the altar, the priests, the prince, the offerings and the land follow. A river flows from under the temple, deepening as it goes, until it makes the Dead Sea fresh: ‘wherever the river flows, everything will flourish’ (47:9). The land is shared among the tribes, and the city is named ‘THE LORD IS THERE’ (48:35).

How to read the vision is debated, and this site takes no side. Some hold that it describes a real temple still to be built, with its worship, in a future age. Some read it as a symbolic picture of God's restored presence among his people, given in the forms a priest would know. Many read it as fulfilled in Christ, who is the true temple, and in the church, where God dwells by his Spirit, and finally in the new creation. Whatever the reading, the vision makes no claim about any modern state, temple or border.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Ezekiel
parts.body:
The New Testament seldom quotes Ezekiel word for word, but Revelation draws on it again and again. It sees four living creatures around the throne (Revelation 4), an angel giving John a scroll that is sweet as honey in the mouth (Revelation 10:9-10), Gog and Magog gathered for battle (Revelation 20:8), a holy city measured on a great high mountain with gates named for the tribes (Revelation 21:10-12), and ‘a river of the water of life’ flowing from the throne, with trees whose leaves are for healing (Revelation 22:1-2). Paul joins words from Leviticus and Ezekiel's promise that God will dwell among his people and be their God (2 Corinthians 6:16).

Christians have also read Jesus' words, ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 10:11), against Ezekiel 34, the new heart of chapter 36 alongside the gift of the Spirit, and the dry bones in the light of the resurrection. These are readings. These notes draw only the lines the New Testament draws.

Read the dates, and follow the glory as it leaves the temple and returns. Read the visions as visions, without forcing them into diagrams. Read the acted signs as preaching. Read chapters 16 and 23 slowly and carefully, as pictures of a city and a covenant, and never as a model for how anyone may treat a woman.

Notice where the book begins and ends. It opens with God appearing to exiles by a canal in Babylon, far from the temple. It closes with a city whose name is ‘THE LORD IS THERE’ (48:35).

hard.line: What did Ezekiel see, and how should a modern reader picture it?
The watchman, and the righteous who turn away.
The prophet lying on his side: a sign-act of the siege.
The killing in the vision of chapter 9, and the mark on those who grieve.
Noah, Daniel and Job: why even they could save only themselves.
Jerusalem pictured as an unfaithful wife: a picture of a city, no warrant to harm any woman.
Sour grapes: each person answers to God, and no suffering is read as deserved.
Oholah and Oholibah: a picture of two cities, no warrant to harm any woman.
The death of Ezekiel's wife, and the command not to mourn.
Tyre's fall, and a siege that did not destroy the island city.
The king of Tyre in Eden: a human king, or Satan?
Dry bones: Israel's return, the resurrection, or both?
Gog of Magog: historical, future or symbolic, with no modern nation named.
The temple vision: a future building, a symbol, or fulfilled in Christ and the church?
Sacrifices in the new temple, and the sacrifice of Christ.

words.line: God's name for Ezekiel, more than ninety times: a mortal, a human being (2:1).
God's visible presence, which leaves the temple and returns (1:28; 10:18; 43:4).
The four beings beneath the throne, later called cherubim (1:5; 10:20).
The canal in Babylonia where the exiles lived and the visions began (1:1).
The one set to warn the city of danger (3:17; 33:7).
A message acted out, such as the siege on a brick (4:1-3).
The book's refrain, that people will know he is the LORD, repeated more than sixty times (6:7).
The proverb that children pay for their parents' sins, which God forbids (18:2).
The two sisters who stand for Samaria and Jerusalem (23:4).
Israel's rulers, condemned for feeding themselves and not the flock (34:2).
God's promise of a heart of flesh in place of stone (36:26).
Ruach, one Hebrew word for all three, which runs through the dry bones (37:9-10).
The leader of the nations gathered against Israel (38:2).
The ruler in the temple vision, with set duties and limits (44:3).
The city's last name, the book's last words (48:35).

timeline.what: Babylon takes King Jehoiachin into exile, and Ezekiel with him (2 Kings 24).
Ezekiel's first vision by the Kebar canal, in the fifth year of the exile (1:2).
The vision of idolatry in the temple (8:1).
The siege of Jerusalem begins, on the usual reckoning (24:1; 2 Kings 25:1).
Babylon takes Jerusalem and burns the temple (2 Kings 25).
A fugitive brings the news: the city has been taken (33:21).
The vision of the new temple, in the twenty-fifth year (40:1).
The last dated word, about Egypt, in the twenty-seventh year (29:17).

places.name: Babylon
places.line: Nebuchadnezzar's capital. Its ruins lie near Hillah in Iraq. The exiles lived in Babylonia, by the Kebar canal (1:1).

places.line: The city Ezekiel said would fall, and whose fall a fugitive reported (33:21).

places.line: The island port pictured as a proud ship (27:3).

places.line: The city whose temple the glory left (11:23), and the city of the last vision (48:35).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: Oholah, the older sister (23:4). Drawn roughly, as a region.

places.name: Sodom
places.line: Named as Jerusalem's sister, whose sin was pride and neglect of the poor (16:49).

places.name: Tyre
places.line: The rich port whose king claimed to be a god (28:2).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: A trading partner of Tyre (27:18), near the northern border of the land (47:16-17).

teaching.mapNote: Every place is at a point this site's maps already use, Babylon at its ruins near Hillah and Samaria roughly, as a region. Tel-abib, the Kebar canal, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Egypt's cities and the borders of chapters 47 and 48 are not placed. No borders are drawn, and the map makes no claim about any border today.
